Blackstone was recording an existing offence, not naming a new one: his own footnotes on this passage cite older authorities ('Kitch. of courts. 20' and '1 Hawk. P. C. 132'). The significance has been rewritten without the 'first' claim.

fieldFixes.summary: The fourth book of William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England (1769) lists eavesdroppers — those who listen under walls, windows or the eaves of a house to pick up talk and then frame slanderous and mischievous tales — among common nuisances. They could be presented at the court-leet or indicted at the sessions, and punished by a fine and by finding sureties for good behaviour. Blackstone was recording an old offence, not creating a new one: his footnotes cite earlier authorities, Kitchin on courts and Hawkins's Pleas of the Crown.
fieldFixes.significance: A common-law offence aimed at listening in, recorded long before 'privacy' was a legal term. The U.S. Supreme Court still cited Blackstone's passage when it confronted electronic eavesdropping in 1967.

issues: The summary says Halpérin notes that twentieth-century French doctrine 'largely ignored' the 1791 provision. His words, in the record's own quote, are 'ignorait totalement' (ignored it entirely). The summary understated the source and has been corrected.

The summary's 'allowed public criticism of officials' is loose. Article 17 permits 'La censure sur les actes des Pouvoirs constitués' (criticism of the acts of the constituted powers) and lets officials prosecute deliberate calumnies against their probity. The wording has been tightened, and the article reference (Title III, ch. V, art. 17), confirmed on both official pages, is added.

fieldFixes.summary: The Constitution of 3 September 1791 (Title III, chapter V, article 17) permitted criticism of the acts of the constituted powers and let officials prosecute deliberate calumnies against their probity. It also provided that calumnies and insults against any person relating to the actions of their private life would be punished at that person's suit. The historian Jean-Louis Halpérin notes that twentieth-century French legal doctrine ignored this provision entirely.

issues: The summary applied the $300 / six-months penalty to any letter an employee 'secreted, embezzled or destroyed'. Section 16 limits that penalty to letters and packets 'which shall not contain any security for, or assurance relating to money'. Secreting, embezzling, destroying or stealing letters containing bank notes, bills or other money instruments carried the death penalty under the same section.

The dead-letter provision is section 18. It applies to letters still unclaimed after being advertised for three months, not to all 'undeliverable' letters. Valuables found were advertised and kept for the addressee on payment of postage. No existing source quoted this provision, so a source is added.

fieldFixes.summary: Section 16 of the Act to establish the Post-Office and Post Roads, approved on 20 February 1792, punished any post-office employee who unlawfully detained, delayed or opened a letter, packet, bag or mail of letters entrusted to him with a fine of up to three hundred dollars, up to six months' imprisonment, or both. The same penalty applied to secreting, embezzling or destroying a letter that held no money or securities. Secreting or stealing letters that contained bank notes or other money instruments was punishable by death. Under section 18, letters still unclaimed after being advertised were sent as 'dead letters' to the General Post Office, where they were opened and inspected, and any valuable papers were advertised and kept for the addressee.

issues: The summary tied the speech to 'the press law that became the law of 17 May 1819'. The primary text (Barante's 1863 edition of Royer-Collard's speeches, pp. 474–475) shows he was speaking to the article 'Nul ne sera admis à prouver la vérité des faits diffamatoires, si ce n'est dans le cas d'imputation contre les dépositaires ou agents de l'autorité ... de faits relatifs à leurs fonctions'. As far as the verifier knows, this rule was enacted as art. 20 of the companion law of 26 May 1819 on prosecution and trial, not the 17 May law; the text of the 1819 laws could not be fetched to confirm the article number. Halpérin speaks loosely of the 17 May law, so the summary now says 'the de Serre press laws of May 1819' and keeps Halpérin's point about 17 May scoped to that law.
Grammar: 'His phrase ... are' is corrected to 'His words ... are'.

The only source was secondary, because the Gallica primary returned HTTP 403. A primary-text source (Barante, via Internet Archive) is added; its quote gives Royer-Collard's own gloss that truth may not be told about private life.

fieldFixes.summary: In the Chamber of Deputies on 27 April 1819, during the debate on the de Serre press laws of May 1819, Royer-Collard defended the bill's rule on proving defamatory facts. Truth could be proved against officials over acts of their public functions, but not against private individuals: 'it is not permitted to tell the truth about private life'. His words — 'voilà donc la vie privée murée ... elle est déclarée invisible, elle est renfermée dans l'intérieur des maisons' — are 'famous' in the historian Jean-Louis Halpérin's phrase. Halpérin also notes that the expression 'vie privée' does not appear in the law of 17 May 1819 itself.
